seoDesc: BIMS (brief interview for mental status): a free health calculator that walks you through 8 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
h1: BIMS (brief interview for mental status) Calculator
summary: The BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator is a free, no-sign-up health tool. Fill in the 7 fields it asks for and it works out BIMS score straight away, with the formula shown underneath. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator work?
sections.html:
The BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports BIMS score in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (able to recall “sock”?, able to recall “blue”? and able to recall “bed”?).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as no word repeated, one word repeated and two words repeated. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as missed by >5 years or no answer, missed by 2 – 5 years and missed by 1 year. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as missed by >1 month or no answer, missed by 6 days to one month and accurate within 5 days. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as incorrect, or no answer and correct. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as no, could not recall, yes, after cueing “something to wear” and yes, no cue required. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as no, could not recall, yes, after cueing “color” and yes, no cue required. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as no, could not recall, yes, after cueing “a piece of furniture” and yes, no cue required. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

7 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

BIMS score=(how many words were repeated correctly? + ask the resident what year it is right now and report their answer + ask the resident what month we are in at the moment and report their answer + ask the resident what day of the week it is today and report their response + able to recall “sock”? + able to recall “blue”? + able to recall “bed”?)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — How many words were repeated correctly? set to All words repeated, Ask the resident what year it is right now and report their answer set to Correct, Ask the resident what month we are in at the moment and report their answer set to Accurate within 5 days and Ask the resident what day of the week it is today and report their response set to Correct — it reports BIMS score = 15.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: BIMS score = 15 should be roughly the size you expected from How many words were repeated correctly? set to All words repeated and Ask the resident what year it is right now and report their answer set to Correct.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns BIMS score. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports BIMS score = 15. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the BIMS (brief interview for mental status) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
